paras: The lynching of Henry Smith took place in July 1881 at Des Arc, Arkansas, when thirty or forty men took the keys from the town's jailer and carried off Smith, a Black prisoner accused of raping and murdering a young orphan girl. They hanged him and threw his body into the river while townspeople followed and no one interfered. Wire briefs carried the story across the country, and Memphis papers openly endorsed the lynching.

According to Little Rock dispatches of July 11, an orphan girl of 13 or 14, raised by a Mr. Stallings, left for school on a Friday morning and never arrived. Searchers hunted all night, and on Saturday morning a man named Winters found her body near a fence, with a bloodied, broken fence rail beside it. The dispatches called her Lucy Webb and said she had been raped and murdered; later reports named her Mattie or Matilda Webb.

Suspicion first fell on two colored men who were said to have left the country. Another version of the dispatch named a Black man, Joe Rymal, as the suspect, possibly with accomplices, and reported that about fifty armed and mounted men were searching for him, "intending to lynch him when caught."

Henry Smith, described as "colored," was then captured; one brief dated his capture to July 11. The Memphis Public Ledger said that after the coroner's inquest a constable and a deputy sheriff brought him to town and lodged him in jail.

The Associated Press account said that about midnight thirty or forty men took the keys from the jailer, entered the jail, and dragged Smith out "into the bright moonlight." They hanged him until he was dead and threw his body into the river, and the dispatch reported that "the people followed them to the river" without anyone trying to stop them. The AP text said that Smith had confessed, a claim that came only from the lynchers' side of the story.

The coverage contains no inquest on Smith's death, no arrests of the lynchers and no grand jury action. According to the AP, "popular sympathy is with the lynchers." No later report on Joe Rymal or the second suspect was found.

The story reached the white press first as a Little Rock murder dispatch on July 12 and then, from July 12 and 13, as a lynching report in papers from Washington to Memphis. The Memphis Daily Appeal headlined it "A NEGRO FIEND," called the lynchers "avenging angels," and described the hanging as "the coolest and most quiet piece of business imaginable." Washington's Evening Critic ran it as "Short Work With a Brute," and the National Republican as "Served Him Right."

Two days later the Memphis Public Ledger conceded that lynching "is dangerous and ought to be prevented," but argued that crimes like that of "the Des Arc fiend" were the circumstance in which it "may be permitted." The same editorial praised Des Arc as a "law-abiding town" whose people had once tarred and feathered two men who insulted a lady and set them adrift on White River in a canoe.

Through late July a one-sentence brief ran in weeklies including the Huntsville Gazette, the Batesville Guard in Arkansas, and the Mineral Point Tribune in Wisconsin, which said only that the people of Des Arc took "a negro ravisher" from jail and hung him to a tree. A condensed version datelined Desarc appeared in Washington's Daily Intelligencer on July 15.

Reports disagreed on the night of the lynching: the AP text and its copies said Saturday night, a shorter brief said Smith was captured on the 11th and lynched that night, and the Daily Republican said Tuesday night. Because the July 11 dispatches still described the suspects as at large, the July 11 date fits the sequence better than Saturday.

The AP and the Memphis Public Ledger said the lynchers wore no masks, while the National Republican reported "forty masked men." Most reports gave the girl's age as 14, but the Evening Critic gave it as 17.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Smith
bases: Thirty or forty men took Henry Smith, a Black prisoner, from the Des Arc jail and hanged him (A5, A17), and every report calls it the work of a mob (A3, A9, A12).
Smith was taken from jail without legal process and hanged by 'thirty or forty' (A5, A17) or 'forty' men (A9) as punishment for the rape and murder of a girl he was accused of (A3, A5).

Separately worded dispatches in the Evening Critic (A3), the Memphis Appeal's AP text (A5), the National Republican (A9) and the Daily Republican (A12) agree that Smith was taken from the Des Arc jail by a mob and hanged, though they differ on the day and on masks.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire, July 11 (before the lynching)
accounts.gist: The girl was raped and killed with a fence rail; suspicion fell on two colored men who had left the country, or on Joe Rymal, and armed men were searching to lynch the culprit.

accounts.label: AP account (Little Rock, July 12)
accounts.gist: After the coroner's inquest Smith was jailed; about midnight Saturday thirty or forty unmasked men took the jailer's keys, hanged him in the moonlight, and threw the body in the river while the people followed; he 'confessed'.

accounts.label: Short wire brief
accounts.gist: Smith was captured on the 11th, lodged in jail, taken out that night by a mob, hanged, cut down and thrown into the river.

accounts.label: National Republican dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of 'forty masked men' took Smith, who had confessed, from the Des Arc jail and hanged him.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'A NEGRO FIEND' and described the lynchers as 'avenging angels', closing 'Popular sympathy is with the lynchers.'
The Memphis Public Ledger editorialized that lynching is dangerous but permissible for crimes like 'the Des Arc fiend's'.
Washington papers used the headlines 'Short Work With a Brute' and 'Served Him Right'.
Weeklies and dailies from Alabama to Wisconsin ran a one-sentence brief without comment.

versions.value: Captured on the 11th, lynched 'last night' in a July 12 dispatch (night of July 11)

conflicts.note: The July 11 dispatches still describe the suspects as at large and a search under way (A1, A19), which fits a lynching on the night of July 11 better than on Saturday the 9th.
The fuller AP text and the Memphis editorial both say no masks.
Mattie may be a short form of Matilda; the age of 17 appears only once.

Rape and murder of a girl aged 13-14 (17 in one report); no paper gives 11.
Supported by the 'captured on the 11th ... last night' reports, but the AP text says Saturday night (July 9) and one brief says Tuesday night (July 12).
A mob that broke into the jail; the armed search party (A19) was a separate, earlier group.
